title: Battery: The Tank
description: Component lesson. A battery is where the whole loop starts — a chemical reaction, packaged, waiting to push electrons for you.

content.value: Every circuit needs something to raise the tank in the first place. That's the battery's whole job: turn stored chemical energy into a steady electrical push, so current has a reason to flow at all.

content.want: A cylindrical 18650 lithium-ion battery cell, photographed on a plain background, label visible
content.caption: ARIA runs on an 18650 cell — the same cylinder shape used in laptop battery packs and power tools.

content.value: Inside, two different chemicals are kept apart by a separator, soaked in an electrolyte. One side wants to give up electrons, the other wants to receive them — but they can only do it through an outside path. Connect a wire between the two ends and that path opens: electrons rush out through the wire, and chemistry keeps the push going until the reaction runs out.

chemical reaction  --push-->  electrons out the (-) terminal
                               through your circuit
                    <--flow--  back in the (+) terminal

"Discharging" is that reaction running forward. "Charging" pushes it back the other way with an outside power source, storing energy again for next time. Not every battery chemistry can be recharged safely — the ones that can, like the 18650, say so on the label.

AA / AAA alkaline   1.5V   cheap, not rechargeable, low current
18650 Li-ion        3.7V   rechargeable, high current, powers ARIA
9V block             9V    handy voltage, weak current, short life
coin cell           3V    tiny devices only (watches, some sensors)

Part          18650 Li-ion cell
Voltage       3.7V nominal (4.2V full, 3.0V empty)
Capacity      ~2600 mAh (can supply 2600 mA for one hour)
Price         ≈ ₹150–250 per cell

Never short the two terminals together with a bare wire — with no resistor or load in the way, current tries to become enormous almost instantly, and the cell gets very hot very fast. Never puncture, crush, or charge a cell with the wrong charger. And check polarity before wiring: connecting a battery backwards can damage whatever it's powering.

content.title: 🔋 Try different voltages
content.hint: Slide the resistor down toward a short — watch how fast the current climbs even before it becomes dangerous.

content.value: Key takeaway: a battery is stored chemistry, released as a steady electrical push (voltage) for as long as the reaction has fuel left.

quiz.question: What actually stops a battery from discharging the instant you make one?
options: Nothing outside the battery is needed — it discharges on its own
The two chemicals can only exchange electrons through an external path, and there isn't one until you wire it
quiz.explain: The chemistry is ready to react, but the electrons need somewhere to go. Without a completed circuit outside the cell, there's no path for them.

quiz.question: Why is shorting a battery's terminals together dangerous?
options: With almost no resistance in the path, the circuit tries to draw a huge current very quickly, heating the cell
It instantly drains the battery to zero with no side effects
quiz.explain: I = V/R — when R collapses toward zero, I shoots toward enormous. That current turns into heat inside the cell, which is exactly the danger.

quiz.question: ARIA's 18650 cell is rated 2600 mAh. Roughly how is that useful to know?
options: It tells you the cell's colour
It estimates how long the cell can supply a given current before it's empty
It has nothing to do with runtime
quiz.explain: mAh (milliamp-hours) is a capacity rating: a 2600 mAh cell can supply roughly 2600 mA for one hour, or 260 mA for ten hours, and so on.
